strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered benchmark spanning 14 datasets across 10 EEG paradigms, 9 models (7 EEG-FMs plus 2 general time-series FMs), and a full factorial design over fine-tuning strategy (frozen/full/LoRA), task setup (single-/multi-task), and classifier head architecture (avg pooling/attention pooling/compressing MLP), addressing a genuine and previously unmet need for standardized EEG-FM evaluation.

Goes beyond simple leaderboard accuracy by introducing a coherent diagnostic toolkit (gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity via PCA, PCGrad-inspired conflict metrics, CKA, RSA) applied consistently across models to probe optimization dynamics, cross-task transfer, and pre-training/fine-tuning objective alignment.

Findings are non-trivial and actionable for the field: multi-task learning as an overfitting regularizer, gradient conflict between reconstruction and classification objectives limiting pre-training efficiency, and violation of naive scaling laws (compact architecturally-biased models like CBraMod outperforming much larger REVE).

Strong reproducibility support: detailed appendices document dataset splits, preprocessing pipeline, training hyperparameters, per-model architectural adaptations, and full result tables (Appx. C) for every configuration, which is unusually thorough for a benchmark submission.

Qualitative analyses (t-SNE, Integrated Gradients topomaps) are tied back to known neurophysiological substrates (e.g., temporal/central channels for spike-wave discharges, frontal/temporal channels for AD), lending some external validity to the learned representations.
weaknesses: The causal narrative built around 'objective misalignment' and 'gradient conflict' driving pre-training inefficiency is inferred from correlational gradient-cosine statistics; no intervention (e.g., modifying the reconstruction objective or reweighting losses) is performed to verify that resolving the identified conflict actually improves downstream transfer, weakening the strength of the mechanistic claims.

The headline 'scaling law violation' conclusion (Fig. 1/11) is drawn from only 7 EEG-FMs with confounded differences in architecture, objective, tokenization, and required model-specific input adapters (Appx. B.6); it is difficult to attribute REVE's underperformance purely to data/parameter scaling versus adaptation artifacts or hyperparameter mismatch, especially since REVE's large pre-training corpus and positional-encoding scheme were forced through a benchmark-specific adapter.

Standardizing all models on a single preprocessing/montage pipeline (Sec. 3.1, Appx. B.1) risks handicapping models whose original pre-training used different sampling rates, referencing, or channel montages, so cross-model comparisons may still partially reflect adaptation quality rather than intrinsic representation quality — a tension acknowledged only implicitly.

Reported results are means ± std over 5 (main) or 10 (diagnostic) seeds without formal significance testing, and several small datasets (e.g., TUSL has only ~40 test trials) make some cross-model rankings statistically fragile despite being discussed as clear trends.

The benchmark's methodological novelty is modest: CKA, RSA, PCGrad-style conflict metrics, and gradient subspace affinity are established techniques repurposed rather than extended; the core contribution is aggregation/engineering rather than new analytic methodology.

Presentation relies heavily on dense radar charts and large heatmap grids explicitly marked 'best viewed via zoom-in,' which hampers readability of the main paper's key comparisons and pushes most quantitative substance into a very long appendix.
The 'Code is available at' link is left as a placeholder in the provided manuscript, so reproducibility cannot be independently verified at review time.

strengths: The benchmark is broad in scope, covering 14 datasets spanning 10 EEG paradigms (motor imagery, sleep staging, emotion recognition, seizure detection, Alzheimer's diagnosis, etc.) and evaluates 7 EEG-FMs plus 2 general time-series models under a unified preprocessing/evaluation pipeline, addressing a genuine reproducibility problem in the field.

The experimental design varies along multiple orthogonal axes (fine-tuning strategy, task setup, classifier head), enabling controlled ablations rather than a single leaderboard number, which is more informative than prior EEG-FM benchmarks.

The diagnostic toolkit (gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity, PCGrad-style conflict measurement, CKA, RSA, Integrated Gradients, t-SNE) goes beyond simple accuracy reporting and attempts to explain mechanisms of transfer, which is a differentiator from prior benchmarks such as MOABB or AdaBrain-Bench.

Extensive appendix with full per-dataset, per-metric results (9 models x 14 datasets x multiple settings) supports transparency and allows readers to inspect raw numbers rather than relying solely on aggregated radar charts.

Some findings are practically useful for practitioners, e.g., that frozen-backbone evaluation substantially understates usable representation quality, and that classifier-head capacity should be matched to task structure rather than uniformly maximized.
weaknesses: The central 'scaling law deviation' claim (Fig. 1, Sec 4.6) is drawn from only 9 points in which architecture, pre-training corpus, objective, and parameter count all vary simultaneously; attributing REVE's underperformance to lack of 'inductive bias' versus confounds (e.g., different adaptation procedure, insufficient hyperparameter tuning per the paper's own grid-search protocol, or task mismatch) is not well isolated and is presented as a general insight rather than a tentative, confound-laden observation.

The gradient/representation diagnostic pipeline compresses gradients via CountSketch hashing to a very low dimension (d=6 in Fig. 8) before computing cosine similarity and conflict statistics; no validation (e.g., comparison to uncompressed gradients, sensitivity to projection dimension/seed) is provided to show this lossy compression preserves the geometric relationships being interpreted, which undermines confidence in claims such as 'reconstruction and classification gradients conflict.'

Several mechanistic claims (e.g., 'pre-training stabilizes the backbone and shifts optimization burden to input embedding,' 'multi-task fine-tuning acts as an attractor guiding scratch models toward pretrained representations') are causal/mechanistic interpretations of correlational visualizations (gradient-norm stacked area charts, CKA/RSA heatmaps) without statistical testing or counterfactual experiments that would support causal attribution.

Reported results carry large standard deviations in many settings (e.g., TUSL, SEED-V, ADFTD kappa values), yet comparative claims across fine-tuning strategies, task setups, and classifier heads in the main text are made qualitatively from radar-chart overlap rather than with explicit significance testing, risking over-claiming distinctions that may not be statistically robust.

Model-specific adaptation procedures differ substantially across EEG-FMs (channel reordering, electrode dropping, convolutional adapters for BENDR/BIOT, flattening for LaBraM/CBraMod, fixed positional encodings for REVE), which, while pragmatic, introduces heterogeneous confounds into a benchmark whose central claim is 'fair' cross-model comparison; the extent to which these adapters differentially help or hurt each architecture is not quantified.
The code repository link in the abstract is empty/placeholder ('Code is available at'), undermining the reproducibility the paper centrally claims to offer at submission time.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not engage with the fact that several benchmarked tasks are clinical (Alzheimer's/FTD diagnosis, seizure detection), where benchmark-driven claims about model reliability could influence downstream clinical-adjacent research without adequate discussion of risks of over-trusting automated EEG classifiers.

Some headline findings (multi-task learning as regularizer, full fine-tuning outperforming frozen probing, high-capacity decoders overfitting) are directionally unsurprising and already anticipated from general transfer-learning literature; the paper's novelty rests more on exhaustive coverage than on fundamentally new conceptual insight.

The diagnostic toolkit's qualitative neurophysiological interpretations in the appendix (e.g., linking Integrated Gradients saliency to 'known' cortical regions for emotion or Alzheimer's) are asserted rather than rigorously validated against ground-truth neuroscience literature or quantitative region-overlap metrics, weakening the strength of the 'diagnostic' contribution claimed in the title.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered benchmark spanning 14 datasets across 10 EEG paradigms, with a unified preprocessing pipeline (filtering, resampling, segmentation, subject-independent splitting) that directly addresses a real reproducibility problem in the EEG-FM literature.

Evaluates a wide and representative set of 9 models (7 EEG-FMs plus 2 general time-series FMs) under three fine-tuning strategies (frozen, full-parameter, LoRA), two task setups (single/multi-task), and three classifier heads, enabling controlled ablations that isolate the effect of each design axis rather than conflating them as prior work does.

Goes beyond end-task accuracy with genuinely novel diagnostic tooling: gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity (via PCA + projection matrix singular values), PCGrad-inspired conflict metrics, CKA and RSA representation analyses, applied consistently across initialization/phase/regime/component axes.

The findings are mechanistically grounded and actionable rather than purely descriptive: e.g., identifying that pre-training stabilizes backbone layers while shifting the optimization burden to the embedding layer, and quantifying gradient conflict between reconstruction and classification objectives as a concrete explanation for inefficient scaling.

Very extensive appendix with full per-dataset, per-metric result tables for every configuration (over a dozen tables), additional model-specific dynamics analyses (CBraMod, CSBrain), and qualitative t-SNE/Integrated Gradients visualizations tied to known neurophysiology, supporting reproducibility and deeper interpretation.

Practical, concrete recommendations for the field (prioritize pre-training objective design over data scaling, adopt multi-task training as default, standardize benchmarking) that follow logically from the presented evidence.
weaknesses: The headline 'scaling law deviation' claim (Fig. 1) rests on only 9 models with heterogeneous architectures, training recipes, and pretraining corpora, so attributing the pattern to 'architectural inductive bias' versus confounded differences in objective, data curation, or hyperparameter tuning is not well isolated; no controlled scaling experiment (e.g., same architecture at multiple sizes/data scales) is provided to support a causal scaling claim.

Gradient-space analyses compress gradients to very low dimensionality (d=6 via CountSketch) before computing cosine similarity/subspace affinity; the impact of this aggressive compression on the fidelity of the reported alignment/conflict statistics is not validated (e.g., no sensitivity analysis across projection dimensions or comparison to uncompressed gradients on smaller models).

Many key figures (radar charts, heatmaps) are dense and rely on 'best viewed via zoom-in,' making the main text's quantitative claims difficult to verify at normal resolution; statistical significance (e.g., confidence intervals on performance differences between fine-tuning strategies) is not explicitly tested despite 5 seeds being run.

The multi-task vs. single-task comparison and classifier-head ablation conclusions are drawn primarily from qualitative radar-chart inspection of 4 representative models rather than systematic aggregate statistics (e.g., win/loss counts or paired significance tests across all 9 models and 14 datasets), slightly weakening the strength of the generalization claims.

Limitations section is relatively brief and does not discuss potential confounds in cross-model comparison (e.g., differing amounts of compute/hyperparameter search per model, which could bias performance rankings), nor the generalizability of findings beyond the specific models studied as new EEG-FMs continue to emerge rapidly.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely problem: EEG foundation model evaluation is fragmented across inconsistent datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and protocols, which the paper documents concretely with citations to specific mismatches in prior work (e.g., EEGPT's frozen linear probe vs. REVE's two-stage fine-tuning vs. CBraMod's fixed-size classifiers).

Very comprehensive experimental scope: 14 datasets across 10 paradigms, 9 models (7 EEG-FMs + 2 general time-series FMs), 3 fine-tuning strategies, 2 task setups, and 3 classifier heads, yielding a large and systematically organized experimental matrix (reflected in the extensive appendix tables C.2-C.9).

Goes beyond simple leaderboard reporting by incorporating genuine diagnostic tooling (gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity via PCA, PCGrad-style conflict metrics, CKA, RSA) to probe optimization dynamics and representation evolution, which is uncommon in benchmark papers and provides mechanistic rather than purely descriptive insights.

Careful handling of potential confounds, such as explicitly flagging and excluding overlap-sensitive model-dataset pairs (e.g., LaBraM/SEED, EEGPT/SEED & PhysioMI) from aggregate performance calculations rather than silently including them.

Findings are non-trivial and actionable for the field: e.g., near-zero/negative gradient alignment between reconstruction and classification objectives suggesting pre-training functions more as "initialization" than semantic transfer, and the observation that nominal scale does not fully explain downstream performance (REVE's large-scale pretraining does not dominate every dataset, while compact models like CBraMod/CSBrain remain competitive).

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed appendix on preprocessing pipeline, dataset splits, training hyperparameters, and model-specific adapters for handling checkpoint-compatible preprocessing, plus stated code availability.

Honest and appropriately scoped limitations section that acknowledges the benchmark's coverage gaps, unified-optimizer suboptimality for heterogeneous tasks, and the fact that EEG-FMs are a moving target.
weaknesses: The core contribution is primarily an evaluation/diagnostic infrastructure rather than a new method or theoretical insight; while valuable, this places a higher bar on the depth and generalizability of the empirical findings, some of which (multi-task helps small datasets but can hurt paradigm-specific tasks; frozen backbones underperform; richer classifier heads help motor imagery) are somewhat expected given prior ML literature on multi-task learning and linear probing.

The many diagnostic-tool hyperparameters (CountSketch projection dim=1024, rank-6 PCA for subspace affinity, probe batch count=32, probing interval) are stated but not extensively justified or ablated for sensitivity, raising some concern about robustness of the gradient/representation-based conclusions.

Cross-model "fair" comparison is complicated by the necessity of model-specific preprocessing/adapters (different normalization conventions, channel reordering, montage handling per model, as detailed in Appendix B.6), which the paper itself acknowledges but does not fully quantify the impact of — this partially undercuts the central claim of a fully standardized, apples-to-apples comparison.

No explicit statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) is reported when comparing models/strategies despite averaging over 5 (or 10) seeds; conclusions about which model or strategy "wins" rest on visual inspection of radar charts and point estimates with std shown separately.

Presentation is dense and, in places, hard to parse: many radar charts and heatmaps are marked "best viewed via zoom-in," and the volume of appendix tables/figures, while thorough, makes it difficult for a reader to extract the highest-priority takeaways without significant effort.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with EEG-specific ethical considerations (e.g., clinical datasets such as ADFTD/Alzheimer's diagnosis, TUAB, dataset consent/privacy, potential misuse or overclaiming of diagnostic capability), which is a missed opportunity given the paper's use of sensitive health-related EEG data.

Some notable recent/relevant EEG-FMs mentioned in related work (Brant-2, LEAD, EEGFormer) are excluded from the actual benchmark evaluation without clear justification for the selection criteria beyond availability, slightly limiting the benchmark's claimed comprehensiveness.

strengths: Substantial engineering effort: 14 datasets spanning 10 EEG paradigms, 7 EEG-FMs plus 2 general time-series baselines, evaluated under a unified preprocessing, splitting, and metric pipeline, which addresses a genuine fragmentation problem in the EEG-FM literature.

The configurable evaluation axes (frozen/full-parameter/LoRA fine-tuning, single- vs multi-task, three classifier heads) enable systematic ablations that go beyond typical single-setting leaderboard comparisons.

The diagnostic toolkit (gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity, PCGrad-style conflict counting, CKA, RSA) is a useful methodological addition for probing optimization dynamics, and is applied consistently across models in the appendix (e.g., CBraMod vs CSBrain comparisons).

Some findings are interesting and plausible from a practitioner's standpoint (frozen-backbone generalization gap, weak gradient alignment between reconstruction and classification objectives, non-monotonic relationship between scale and downstream performance), and the paper is transparent about overlap-sensitive dataset/model pairs.

Extensive appendix with full per-dataset numeric tables, qualitative t-SNE/Integrated-Gradients visualizations, and documented training/preprocessing details support reproducibility to a reasonable degree.
weaknesses: Limited methodological or scientific novelty: the core contribution is a benchmarking/evaluation harness rather than a new model, objective, or theoretical insight; the diagnostic metrics used (CKA, RSA, PCGrad-style conflict, subspace affinity) are all adopted wholesale from prior work with no adaptation specific to the EEG setting, and the headline conclusions (multi-task can help/hurt depending on compatibility, frozen backbones underperform, scale doesn't fully explain transfer, reconstruction and classification objectives can conflict) largely recapitulate well-established general ML findings rather than producing new, EEG-specific understanding.

The claimed 'fair comparison' is undermined by the fact that each model requires bespoke, model-specific adapters, channel reordering schemes, and normalization conventions (Appx B.6) to remain checkpoint-compatible; these unavoidable per-model choices are acknowledged as a limitation but their quantitative impact on the cross-model rankings is never isolated or ablated, so it is unclear how much of the reported performance differences reflect genuine representation quality versus adapter/preprocessing idiosyncrasies.

The pre-training data size used in the headline scaling plot (Fig. 1) is a rough proxy ('estimated based on total duration of the raw data signal'), and no independent reproduction check is reported to confirm that the reimplemented models match their originally published numbers, raising concerns about whether reported gaps are implementation artifacts (e.g., CSBrain's extreme instability from scratch, Fig. 25) rather than genuine architectural or pre-training effects.

No new method, objective, or architecture is proposed to address the identified bottlenecks (gradient conflict, negative transfer, generalization gap); all actionable recommendations are deferred to 'future work,' limiting the paper's constructive contribution beyond diagnosis.

Presentation is heavily overloaded: nearly every multi-panel radar chart and heatmap figure is accompanied by 'best viewed via zoom-in,' and many figures are essentially impossible to read at normal resolution (e.g., the 6x6 per-component gradient correlation matrices, 14-axis radar charts with overlapping confidence bands), reducing the practical interpretability of the diagnostic claims drawn from them.

Statistical rigor is thin: reported standard deviations for many comparisons (e.g., Tables 2–9) are large relative to the differences being discussed (e.g., single- vs multi-task, frozen vs LoRA), yet no significance testing or effect-size analysis is used to support claims of 'negative transfer' or ranking differences between models.

The neurophysiological interpretation of Integrated-Gradients topomaps (Appx E) is purely qualitative/anecdotal, with no quantitative validation against known neurophysiology, weakening the strength of claims that model attention 'aligns with' known brain regions.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered benchmark infrastructure covering 14 datasets across 10 EEG paradigms, 7 EEG-FMs plus 2 general time-series models, with three fine-tuning strategies, two task setups, and three classifier heads - a much-needed standardization effort given the fragmented evaluation landscape described in related work.

Goes substantially beyond simple leaderboard-style benchmarking by introducing genuine diagnostic tooling (gradient cosine similarity, subspace affinity via PCA, CKA, RSA, PCGrad-inspired conflict metrics) that is applied consistently across models and settings, yielding mechanistic insights (e.g., gradient conflict between reconstruction and classification objectives, normalization/temporal-embedding layers as task-agnostic shared subspaces) that are more interesting than raw accuracy numbers.

Thoughtful handling of practical confounds: explicit flagging and exclusion of overlap-sensitive model-dataset pairs (e.g., LaBraM/SEED, EEGPT/SEED+PhysioMI) from aggregate metrics, detailed model-specific adaptation/preprocessing notes to preserve checkpoint compatibility, and a very extensive appendix with full per-dataset, per-strategy result tables (Tables 2-9) supporting the main-text claims.

Multiple complementary analyses converge on a coherent narrative (frozen-backbone generalization gap, multi-task regularization vs. negative transfer, scale not fully explaining transfer performance, objective misalignment via gradient geometry) rather than isolated findings, and the qualitative visualizations (t-SNE, Integrated Gradients topomaps) in the appendix lend some neurophysiological plausibility to the quantitative patterns.

Reasonable reproducibility: detailed training hyperparameters, data splitting protocols per dataset, evaluation metric definitions, and stated intent to maintain the benchmark as infrastructure; code availability is mentioned (though not verifiable here).
weaknesses: The core empirical claims rest heavily on a single run (or limited seeds) for diagnostic/gradient analyses per the text ("Using LaBraM... as a case" for Fig. 3/4, though probing claims 10 seeds for dynamics) while performance tables use 5 seeds; given the generally large standard deviations visible throughout (e.g., Table 2-9, many datasets show overlapping error bars across models/strategies), several comparative claims (e.g., REVE being "strongest" overall, specific negative-transfer claims per paradigm) may not be statistically robust, and no significance testing is reported.

The gradient/representation diagnostic analyses (Figs. 3-4, 7-8, 15-25) are presented almost entirely qualitatively ("shows high correlation," "suggests task-agnostic dynamics") without statistical tests, effect sizes, or ablations isolating confounds (e.g., parameter-group size differences could trivially affect gradient-norm or CKA comparisons), limiting how strongly the mechanistic conclusions can be trusted versus being suggestive post-hoc narratives.

Benchmark design choices embed many researcher degrees of freedom (per-model preprocessing/scaling conventions, differential learning rates, grid search per model, subject-dependent vs. independent splits by dataset) that, while reasonably justified, could still differentially advantage certain models; the paper acknowledges this only briefly in Limitations without quantifying sensitivity to these choices.

Despite the claim of 'comprehensive' coverage, the benchmark is restricted to classification tasks on public datasets with released checkpoints, excludes regression/generative or multimodal EEG settings, and the 'from-scratch' and single-task baselines sometimes show training instability (e.g., CSBrain collapse, Fig. 25) that is noted as an aside rather than systematically investigated, raising questions about whether some reported scratch/overlap comparisons are reliable.

Presentation is dense and visually taxing, especially radar charts (Figs. 5,6,9,10) with many overlapping lines and small text that are explicitly flagged as needing zoom-in, and the large number of near-duplicate figures in the appendix (per-model versions of Figs. 3-4) somewhat dilute focus without adding proportionate insight beyond what is in the main text.
